script.opening_words: Gasoline costs about 30% more than it did a year ago. Diesel, the fuel that moves everything you own, is near its all-time record. And nobody at the Federal Reserve can do a thing about either one. Not because they're bad at their jobs, because interest rates don't drill oil. I filled up on Tuesday. 14 gallons, 57 bucks. A year ago, that same tank was $44. And here's what most people haven't connected. The gas, the grocery bill, the
script.ending_words: loses, the crowded trade that already won, and the price you're paying while everybody argues about the other two. Tell me where you land. Does this rhyme with 1973, or is the comparison nonsense? I'd rather be argued with than agreed with. And if this was useful, send it to somebody who's been quietly worried about money and hasn't said so out loud. I'll see you in the next one.
script.analysis: Full 18398 canonical characters read. A historical-comparison essay: gas-price hook; Nixon shock and price controls; OPEC embargo; the Rileys (composite family); trap one: safe money (1970s inflation, T-bills, Regulation Q, 1973-74 crash, flat Dow 1966-82, mortgage rate shock 7.5% vs 18.63%); trap two: crowded trade (gold 1971-80-99, energy weight); 2026 parallels (Iran/Hormuz, debt, interest, Fed, real wages, gold and silver drawdowns); trap three: entry price (1982 CAPE 6.5 vs ~41, yields 6.24% vs 1.05%, concentration, Polaroid); counter-arguments (anchored 5y5y expectations, low unionisation, US oil production); age-dependent implications; Rileys' DCA and $804,000; close. FRED-verified: 1970s inflation peaks and cumulative figures, 18.63% mortgage record, both mortgage payments, 5y5y 2.32%, debt level. Overstated: debt growth "$91,549 per second". 2026 geopolitical and precious-metal figures unverified. The stored ending is complete.
